lessons.intro: French writes letters it never says. Not a few odd ones: most final consonants, every H, and the final -E all sit on the page in silence. This lesson gives you one default and four overrides, so that any French word you have never seen before, on a menu, a street sign, a train ticket, comes out of your mouth close to right on the first try.

ipa.body: Sounds appear two ways in this course. IPA sits between slashes and is exact, the same alphabet linguists use worldwide: /pə.ti/. The respelling sits between brackets and is a reading aid for an English speaker, with the stressed syllable capitalised: [pə-TEE]. When the two disagree, trust the IPA. A small raised n, as in [GRAHⁿ], marks a nasal vowel: it means the vowel is sent through the nose, NOT that you should say an N.
ipa.title: The two notations, and what each is for

hMuet.body: Muet means mute. No H is ever pronounced in French, so this is not about sound at all: it is about grammar. An H muet behaves as though the letter were simply not there, so the word in front of it elides in the normal way. Le plus homme becomes l'homme, exactly as le plus arbre becomes l'arbre. Most French H words are muet.
hMuet.title: H muet: the H that lets the article shrink

careful.body: Most final consonants in French are silent. Four of them usually are not: C, R, F and L. Spell those four out and you get the English word CaReFuL, which is the whole point of the name: it is a memory hook, not a French word. When you reach the end of a word you have never seen, ask one question. Is the last letter C, R, F or L? If yes, say it. If no, stay quiet. That single question gets you most of the way, every time, and the rest of this lesson is the handful of cases where it needs help.
careful.title: CaReFuL: the four letters that stay awake

eSwitch.body: A final -e is itself silent. It is never a syllable, so porte is one sound, PORT, and never POR-tuh. What it does is wake the consonant standing in front of it. grand ends on a nasal vowel with a silent D; add the -e and grande releases a real D at the end. This is why French gender is audible: a hard consonant at the end of an adjective usually means there is an -e behind it, which usually means feminine. Your ears can do grammar.
eSwitch.title: The final -e: an alarm clock for the letter before it

hAspire.body: Aspiré means breathed, and the name is misleading: an H aspiré is NOT breathed and makes no sound, exactly like an H muet. The only difference is grammatical. An H aspiré blocks the elision, so the article stays whole: le héros, not l'héros. There is no way to hear which kind an H is from the word alone. You learn it with the article, the same way you learn a noun with its gender.
hAspire.title: H aspiré: the H that blocks elision

liaison.body: These silent finals are sleeping, not dead. When the next word begins with a vowel, some of them come back and link across the gap: deux euros is said /dø.zø.ʁo/, with the X of deux returning as a Z. That linking is called liaison, and it is the whole of your next lesson. For now it is enough to know why French bothers writing letters it does not say: because sometimes it does say them.
liaison.title: Liaison: when a silent letter wakes up

examples.note: the Z here is a liaison

erEnding.body: CaReFuL says an R at the end of a word should sound. That is right about half the time, and wrong on every verb in the language. The reason is that -er is not a word ending, it is a GRAMMATICAL ending: it marks an infinitive (parler, manger, to speak, to eat) or a job noun (boulanger, a baker). Grammatical endings follow their own rule, and this one is pronounced as a single /e/ with the R completely silent. Short standalone words like hiver and mer are not carrying an ending at all, so their R stays alive.
erEnding.title: The -er ending: where CaReFuL stops applying

silentEnt.body: Four letters, two completely different jobs. On a conjugated verb, -ent is entirely silent: ils parlent is /il paʁl/ and sounds exactly like il parle. On a noun or an adverb it is a real nasal vowel: vent, content and comment all end in /ɑ̃/. There is one question that separates them. Is this a conjugated verb? If yes, the ending is silent. If no, you hear it.
silentEnt.title: The -ent ending: silent on a verb, sounded on anything else

sections.body: No H is ever pronounced in French. The two kinds differ in one thing only: whether the word in front of them elides. H muet takes l' and links; H aspiré keeps le or la and blocks the link.
sections.title: The only difference that matters
H aspiré: keeps le or la

sections.body: héros is aspiré but héroïne is muet, which is genuinely irregular. onze, oui, yaourt and huit behave like aspiré words without having an H at all: le onze, le yaourt, le huit.
sections.title: The oddities

sheets.title: Why French writes what it does not say
contains: why silent letters still have jobs

sections.body: Old French said most of these letters. Between roughly the 12th and 16th centuries the endings stopped being pronounced, and the spelling did not follow, partly because printers had already fixed it and partly because scholars deliberately kept the Latin shape visible. temps keeps its P and S from Latin tempus. doigt gained its G from digitus centuries after anyone said it.
sections.title: They used to be pronounced

sections.body: A silent letter is not decoration. It separates homophones on the page, marks gender and number that the ear cannot hear, and wakes up in liaison before a vowel. Remove the S from les amis and you lose the plural entirely.
sections.title: What they still do
Homophone sets the spelling keeps apart

sheets.title: How to read the sounds in this course

sections.body: IPA sits in slashes and is exact: /pə.ti/. The respelling sits in brackets and is a reading aid for an English speaker, with the stressed syllable capitalised: [pə-TEE]. When they disagree, the IPA is right.
sections.title: Two notations, two jobs

sections.body: A nasal vowel is one sound made through the nose. It is not a vowel plus an N. Writing [GRAHN] tells you to close your mouth on a consonant that French never says, which is the exact error this lesson exists to remove, so the superscript marks the nasality without ever spelling a consonant.
sections.title: Why the superscript matters

rows: from the throat, never the tongue tip

overview.introFr: En français, beaucoup de lettres s'écrivent mais ne se prononcent pas. Ce sont surtout les consonnes finales, le H et le -E final. Dans cette leçon, vous apprenez une règle par défaut et quatre exceptions.

goals.s: Read petit, grand, beaucoup, Paris and trop aloud without adding a single sound French does not make.
Sound the C, R, F and L that stay awake at the end of a word: sac, hiver, chef, avril.
Say parler and boulanger with a silent R, while keeping the R alive in hiver and mer.
Start l'hôtel and l'homme straight on the vowel, and know why le héros keeps its full article.
Tell grand from grande and petit from petite by ear alone, with no other clue in the sentence.
Say ils parlent so it sounds exactly like je parle, because it does.
Meet a French word you have never seen, on a menu or a sign, and get its ending right on the first attempt.

cards.head: Silent unless there's a reason.
cards.body: That is the whole lesson in five words. A final consonant is silent until something specific overrides it.

cards.head: French words are shorter out loud
cards.body: Almost always. beaucoup is eight letters and two syllables. vraiment is eight letters and two. If your mouth is busier than the page, you have added something.

cards.head: CaReFuL: C, R, F, L
cards.body: Four letters that usually survive at the end of a word: sac, hiver, chef, avril. Spell them out and you get the English word CaReFuL.

cards.head: CaReFuL is the exception that counts
cards.body: Every other final consonant stays silent. These four are the reason the rule says usually, so when a final consonant does sound, check this list first.

cards.head: H is a ghost
cards.body: Never a sound, anywhere in French, in any position. It does still change the words around it, and that split has its own name later in the lesson.

cards.head: A final -E is an alarm clock
cards.body: Silent itself, but it wakes the consonant standing in front of it. grand becomes grande, and now you can hear the D.

cards.head: Silent, not dead
cards.body: Silent unless there is a reason, and the next word can be the reason. Those sleeping consonants wake before a vowel. That is liaison, and it is the next lesson.

say.text: One rule, and it decides every verb you will ever read.

sections.body: hiver, mer, cher: short words, R alive. parler, manger, boulanger: the -er ending is just /e/, and the R is gone. Silent unless there's a reason. Being a short word is the reason.

sections.intro: Your eyes see the last letter and your mouth starts loading it before you have decided anything. That happens in about a fifth of a second, which is faster than any rule you can consciously apply. So the rule has to become a reflex, and reflexes are built by doing, not reading.
sections.title: Training the stop

closing.text: Do the finger stop on the first three French words you see tomorrow, on any sign or label. Silent unless there's a reason. Thirty seconds a day beats an hour once.

targets.sub: For any word ending in a default-silent letter
targets.label: The finger stop
steps: Read the word silently, all the way to the end.
Put a finger over the final letter so you cannot see it.
Say only what is left on the page.
Take the finger away and say it again exactly the same way. Do not let the letter back in.
Repeat until step four sounds like step three with no effort.

targets.sub: For words that must end open
targets.label: The vowel landing
steps: Say the word and hold the last sound for two full seconds.
If you can hold it, it is a vowel and you are correct.
If it stops dead, you closed on a consonant that should not be there.
Try again and land on the vowel like a step you are settling onto, not a door you are shutting.

targets.sub: For the masculine and feminine pair
targets.label: The switch check
steps: Say the masculine form. It should end open, on a vowel.
Now say the feminine. Release the woken consonant cleanly and stop.
Do not add a small uh after it. The -e is silent, it is only the switch.
Alternate the pair six times without pausing between them.

say.text: Every French teacher hears these eight, every week, from every English speaker. None of them are careless. Each one is a good instinct pointed at the wrong language.

errors.why: English says nearly every letter it writes. Cat ends in a real T. Your reading reflex was built on a language where the last letter is a promise, and French breaks that promise on most words.
errors.right: petit /pə.ti/ [pə-TEE]
errors.wrong: petit said as [pə-TEET]

errors.why: A final P is unusual enough in English that when you see one you make sure to pronounce it. That extra care is exactly what gives you away here.
errors.right: beaucoup /bo.ku/ [boh-KOO]
errors.wrong: beaucoup said as [boh-KOOP]

errors.why: You learned CaReFuL and applied it faithfully. The problem is that -er is a grammatical ending, not a word ending, and endings follow their own rule. Being consistent is what led you astray.
errors.right: parler /paʁ.le/ [par-LAY]
errors.wrong: parler said as [par-LEHR]

errors.why: This is over-correction, and it usually shows up in week three. You learned that French drops final consonants and started dropping all of them. The default is strong, not absolute.
errors.right: sac /sak/ [SAK]
errors.wrong: sac said as [SA]

errors.why: English H is a real sound and it is at the front of the word, where your mouth commits before you have thought. You are not adding a letter, you are failing to remove a habit.
errors.right: l'hôtel /lo.tɛl/ [lo-TEL]
errors.wrong: hôtel said with a breath, [HO-tel]

errors.why: You have heard French sung, or heard southern French, where the final -e does get a small vowel. It is real, it is just not standard spoken French, and it adds a syllable that changes the rhythm of the whole sentence.
errors.right: porte /pɔʁt/ [PORT]
errors.wrong: porte said as [POR-tuh]

errors.why: You met -ent in comment and vent, where it genuinely is a nasal /ɑ̃/. Then you met it on a verb and applied what you already knew. Same four letters, two completely different jobs.
errors.right: ils parlent /il paʁl/ [eel PARL]
errors.wrong: ils parlent said as [eel par-LAHⁿ]

errors.why: You applied the silent-S default correctly and got a real French word, just the wrong one. fil is thread. This is one of about six words you simply have to bank, and the rules will not save you.
errors.right: fils /fis/ [FEES]
errors.wrong: fils said as [FEEL]

sections.body: An hour ago the ending of a French word was a coin toss. Now you have a default, four overrides and a short list of stubborn words. That is the entire system, and the rest of French pronunciation builds directly on top of it. The R was the hard one and you have been through it twice, from both ends: producing it in the trap drill, hearing it in the listening drill.

questions.q: Which word keeps its final consonant?
questions.why: avec /a.vɛk/. C is a CaReFuL letter. The other three end in silent T, D and P.

questions.q: The R of « boulanger » is:
questions.why: A job noun in -er. The whole ending is /e/ and the R is silent, exactly like an infinitive.

questions.q: Odd one out. Which one has a SILENT final R?
questions.why: premier /pʁə.mje/ is in the -ier family. hier looks like it belongs there and does not: /jɛʁ/, R sounded.

questions.q: Tap the letter you do not say.
questions.why: The -er ending is one /e/. /paʁ.le/. Note the first R does sound.

questions.q: Which word did you hear?
questions.why: A clear K at the end. sac /sak/, CaReFuL C.

questions.q: Which word did you hear?
questions.why: clef /kle/ ends open. Its F is silent, which makes it an exception to CaReFuL. chef /ʃɛf/ keeps its F.

questions.q: A learner says [ee-VAY] for « hiver ». Fix it.
questions.why: They applied the -er rule to a short noun. hiver keeps its R. Only infinitives and job nouns drop it.

say.text: Round three. The letter that makes no sound and still changes the word in front of it.

questions.q: In which of these do you pronounce an H sound?
questions.why: French never pronounces H, in any word, in any position. Muet and aspiré differ in grammar, not in sound.

questions.q: Which noun keeps its full article, with no elision?
questions.why: haricot has an H aspiré: le haricot. The other three are muet and take l'.

questions.q: In « les hommes », the liaison:
questions.why: H muet behaves as though it were not there, so the S of les links across as a /z/.
opts: turns the H into a real sound

questions.q: Tap the letter you do not say.
questions.why: /o.tɛl/. Straight onto the vowel, no puff of air. The L at the end does sound.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: No /z/ between the words. The H aspiré of héros blocks the liaison, leaving a small gap.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: One unbroken sound, /lɔm/. The article has elided, so this is an H muet word.

questions.q: A learner writes « le homme ». Fix it.
questions.why: homme has an H muet, so the article must elide. Blocking elision here is the mirror of wrongly eliding before héros.

questions.q: Type the article that goes in front of « héros ».
questions.why: H aspiré. No elision, no liaison, and still no H sound. The article is the only clue you get.

say.text: Last round. The letter that wakes others up, and the handful of words that ignore everything you have learned.

questions.q: What does a silent final -e do to the consonant before it?
questions.why: grand /ɡʁɑ̃/ becomes grande /ɡʁɑ̃d/. The E stays silent and the D starts sounding.

questions.q: You hear a clear T at the end of an adjective. It is probably:
questions.why: A sounded final consonant usually means an -e woke it, and that -e is the feminine marker. Your ears can do grammar.

questions.q: Which pair sounds IDENTICAL?
questions.why: The plural -s is silent, so the noun does not change. Only the article carries the number.

questions.q: Tap the letters you do not say.
questions.why: /il paʁl/. All four letters of -ent go silent on a conjugated verb. Stop after the L.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: A /z/ at the end. The final -e woke the S, and a woken S between vowels comes out as /z/.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: fils /fis/ ends in an S sound, which the default says should not happen. It is one of about six words you memorise.

questions.q: A learner says [PAR-lahⁿ] for « ils parlent ». Fix it.
questions.why: They borrowed the /ɑ̃/ from comment and vent, where -ent really is nasal. On a verb, all four letters are silent.

questions.q: Say it: « Elle est grande. »
questions.why: Release the D and stop. No small uh after it: the -e is a switch, not a syllable.

say.text: That is the lesson. Six things worth keeping, and the last one is where you go next.

sections.body: An hour ago you sounded the x in deux and a woman in a bakery could not understand you. The fix was not a longer list of words. It was one default and four overrides, and you now run them without thinking about most of them. From here, every new French word you meet has a first guess attached to it before you even try to say it. That is the difference between reading French and decoding it.
sections.title: What you take with you
points: Silent unless there's a reason. That is your default for every final consonant, on every word, forever.
CaReFuL: C, R, F, L are the reason, most of the time. sac, hiver, chef, avril.
The -er ending overrules CaReFuL. parler and boulanger drop the R. hiver and mer keep it.
H is a ghost. Never a sound. It only decides whether the article shrinks: l'homme against le héros.
A silent final -e is an alarm clock for the consonant in front of it, and that is how you hear gender.
Those silent finals are sleeping, not dead. Before a vowel, some of them wake up: deux‿euros, petit‿ami. That is liaison, and it is your next lesson.

errorTriggers.description: Sounds a final consonant that should be silent: the T in petit, the P in beaucoup, the S in Paris, the X in deux.
Drops a CaReFuL final that should sound (sac becomes /sa/), or over-applies CaReFuL to the -er ending (parler becomes /paʁ.lɛʁ/).
Breathes the H, or mixes up muet and aspiré: elides before héros, blocks elision before homme.
Pronounces a final -e as its own syllable (porte becomes /pɔʁ.tə/), or fails to sound the consonant it wakes (grande stays /ɡʁɑ̃/).
Applies a rule to one of the memorised exceptions: says /fil/ for fils, /tu/ for the pronoun tous, /nɛ/ for net.

lessons.intro: French greetings split along a single line: tu or vous. Get that one choice right and « bonjour », « merci » and « au revoir » will carry you through almost any first exchange.
lessons.title: Les salutations

overview.introFr: En français, tout commence par un choix : tu ou vous. Apprenez à saluer, à demander comment ça va, à remercier et à prendre congé, poliment ou entre amis.

detail.body: The universal daytime greeting, and the safest word in French. It works with anyone, in any setting, formal or not. In a shop it is close to obligatory.
detail.title: Bonjour

detail.body: French switches over to bonsoir once evening begins, roughly 6pm. Using bonjour after dark sounds like you did not notice the time.
detail.title: Bonsoir

detail.body: Casual only. It means both hi and bye. Never use it with a boss, a stranger, or anyone you address as vous.
detail.title: Salut

detail.body: The standard goodbye. Safe everywhere, exactly like bonjour is on the way in.
detail.title: Au revoir

detail.body: Only for actual sleep. It is not an evening greeting, it is what you say last, on the way to bed.

sections.text: Il est huit heures. Madame Colin sort de son appartement. Dans l’ascenseur, elle voit son voisin. « Bonjour monsieur, comment allez-vous ? » « Ça va bien, merci, et vous ? » « Très bien ! » Ils arrivent en bas. « Bonne journée, madame ! » « Merci, à demain ! » Dans la rue, elle voit son ami Marc. « Salut Marc ! Ça va ? » « Salut ! Ça va, et toi ? »
sections.title: A Morning in the Building

questions.a: « Bonjour monsieur, comment allez-vous ? » She uses vous, because he is a neighbour, not a close friend.
questions.q: What does Madame Colin say to her neighbour in the lift?

questions.a: Marc is her friend, so she uses tu and the casual greeting. The neighbour gets vous and bonjour.
questions.q: Why does she say « salut » to Marc but not to her neighbour?

questions.a: « Bonne journée » and « à demain », so they expect to see each other again tomorrow.
questions.q: How do the neighbour and Madame Colin part?

cards.back: Daytime, anyone, anywhere. The safest word in French.
Casual only. Means both hi and bye. Never with vous.
The standard goodbye, safe in every register.
Only for going to sleep. Not an evening greeting.
Leaving in the evening. This is the one people mix up with bonne nuit.
Friends, family, children take tu. Everyone else takes vous. When unsure, vous.
Question and answer both. The workhorse of casual French.
The vous version of ça va. Formal, and always paired with bonjour.
Thank you, and the everyday reply. Je vous en prie is the formal reply.
Please, in vous and tu. Same phrase, one word swapped.

sections.say: A quick look at how far you have come in one lesson.
sections.body: You can now open a conversation, ask how someone is, give your name, say thank you, and take your leave, in both registers. That is a complete first exchange, and it is the hardest one to start.
sections.title: Where You Stand

questions.q: You are greeting your new boss at 9am. You say...
questions.why: A boss takes vous, and it is morning. Salut would be far too familiar.

questions.q: Which one is the casual way to say goodbye?
questions.why: Salut works at both ends of a casual conversation, hello and goodbye.

questions.q: You are leaving a dinner party at 10pm. You say...
questions.why: Bonne soirée wishes someone a good evening. Bonne nuit is only for going to sleep.

questions.q: A client thanks you at work. The formal reply is...
questions.why: De rien is casual. In a professional setting, je vous en prie is the polite reply.

questions.q: « Comment allez-vous ? » is asked to...
questions.why: The allez-vous form is the vous form. With a friend you would say « ça va ? ».

questions.q: You walk into a boulangerie. What comes first?
questions.why: Bonjour always comes first in France. Naming what you want straight away reads as abrupt.

questions.q: Which is the correct answer to « Ça va ? »
questions.why: Ça va is both the question and the answer. Only the tone changes.

questions.q: « Je m’appelle » means...
questions.why: Literally "I call myself". It is how French gives a name.

questions.q: Someone says « Enchanté ». What just happened?
questions.why: Enchanté is what you say on meeting someone for the first time.

questions.q: Which greeting works ONLY on the telephone?
questions.why: Allô is for answering a call. Using it face to face would sound strange.

questions.q: Your friend is struggling with a heavy box. You ask « Ça va ? ». You mean...
questions.why: Ça va also works as a check that someone is alright.

questions.q: When you are not sure whether to use tu or vous, you should...
questions.why: Vous is never wrong. Too much distance is easy to fix, too little is not.

lessons.intro: Every letter's real sound. Learn the French name and the in-word sound of all 26 letters, master the ones that trip up English speakers, and spell your own name and email aloud with total confidence.
lessons.title: L'alphabet français

overview.subFr: L'alphabet : le vrai son de chaque lettre
overview.introFr: Apprenez le nom et le vrai son des 26 lettres, maîtrisez celles qui piègent les anglophones, et épelez votre nom et votre email à voix haute avec une confiance totale.
overview.titleEn: The French Alphabet: Every Letter's Real Sound

sections.say: Here is a moment that catches almost every learner off guard. You are on the phone with a hotel in Lyon, and the receptionist asks for your email. You start spelling: P, A, U, L. And there is a long pause. She wrote down something completely different, because the letter you call AY is actually the French E, and the letter you call EE is the French I. The good news? This is a small, closed skill. Twenty six letters, they never change, and after this lesson you will own every one of them.
sections.body:
You are on the phone with a hotel in Lyon, and the receptionist asks for your email. You start reading it out: P, A, U, L. There is a long pause. She heard pay, ah, oo, ell, and wrote down something completely different, because in French the letter you call AY is actually E, and the letter you call EE is I. Two minutes later you still do not have your confirmation.

That exact moment happens to travellers every day: dictating an email, spelling a last name at a pharmacy, giving a booking reference. The good news: this is a small, closed skill. There are only 26 letters, they never change, and once you own them you can spell anything in French.
sections.title: Why this matters

sections.say: By the end of this lesson you will be able to name all twenty six letters the French way, keep a letter's name and its sound in separate boxes, survive the ambush letters, and spell your own name and email out loud, slowly and clearly, like a local.
sections.title: What you'll master
points: Say the French name of all 26 letters, the way a French person spells out loud.
Tell a letter's NAME (for spelling) from its SOUND (inside words), the mix-up beginners make most.
Handle the ambush letters: E, G, H, I, J, R, U, W, Y and the vowels.
Say double vé for W and i grec for Y like a local, instead of guessing.
Spell your own name out loud in French, slowly and clearly.
Dictate an email address in French, including the @, the dot, and the tricky letters.
Recognise the French alphabet song and why its ending sounds different.

sections.say: Here is the one idea that fixes half your mistakes. A letter has two separate jobs. Its name is what you say when you spell out loud. Its sound is the noise it makes inside a word. When you dictate your email, you use names. When you read a word aloud, you use sounds. Keep those two jobs in separate boxes in your head, and most of the confusion disappears.
sections.body:
A letter has two completely separate jobs, and beginners jam them together.

The NAME of a letter is what you say when you spell a word out loud, letter by letter. The SOUND is the noise it makes inside a word: the B in boat does not go bee, it goes a short buh.

French works the same way. When you dictate your email, you use names. When you read a French word aloud, you use sounds.

KEY RULE: Spelling out loud = letter NAMES. Reading a word = letter SOUNDS. Different tools for different jobs.
sections.title: The core concept: name versus sound

sections.say: A quick note on how sounds are written in this lesson. Every sound appears three ways: the precise phonetic symbol in slashes, a plain sounds-like hint, and a respelling in brackets with the stressed syllable in capitals. One special code to remember: z h means the soft buzzy sound in the middle of measure. Hold onto that, it is the key to the letters G and J.

rows.v: The precise symbols in slashes, like /a/. An anchor, not homework.

detail.body: The International Phonetic Alphabet gives every sound in every language its own exact symbol, so /a/ always means the same thing no matter what language you're reading it in. You never need to memorize the IPA to use this course: it's here as a precise anchor you can check against, not something to study on its own. Whenever the plain-English hint feels ambiguous, the IPA symbol next to it is the exact answer.
detail.title: IPA

rows.v: A plain English hint: ah as in father.

detail.body: The fastest way in: a short comparison to a sound you already make in English, like ah as in father. It gets you close enough to be understood on the first try. It is deliberately approximate, because French vowels and English vowels are never perfectly identical, which is exactly why every sound also gets the more precise IPA symbol and the respelling alongside it.
detail.title: Sounds like

rows.v: A respelling with the stressed syllable in CAPS: bonjour is [bon-ZHOOR].

detail.body: A respelling breaks a French word into rough English-readable chunks, with the syllable you stress hardest written in CAPS: bonjour becomes [bon-ZHOOR]. French stress is much flatter than English stress overall, but the last syllable of a phrase still lands a little heavier, and the capitalized chunk is your cue for where that is.
detail.title: [brackets]

rows.v: The soft buzz in the middle of measure or vision. The key to G and J.

detail.body: One special code worth memorizing on its own: zh is the soft, buzzy sound in the middle of the English words measure or vision: not a hard j, and not an h. It shows up constantly in French, and it is the exact sound both G (before E, I, Y) and J make. Say "mesure" slowly and feel where your tongue sits for that middle sound. That's zh.
detail.title: zh

sections.title: How sounds are written here

sections.say: These are the traps, the letters that ambush English speakers. Spend most of your time here. Swipe through each card, listen, and say each French word out loud. The two biggest offenders: E, which is uh and never ee. And the great G J swap: G goes AY, J goes EE.

cards.body: Its name is a soft uh: relaxed, half-open mouth. The English instinct is to call E ee, but that is the French letter I. Inside words French E is often so light it nearly vanishes. Burn it in: E is uh, I is ee.
cards.head: E is [uh], never ee
cards.label: THE TRAP · E

cards.body: In English, G is jee and J is jay. French flips it: G is [zhay], J is [zhee]. Both start with the soft zh of measure, with no hidden d at the front. Remember: G goes AY, J goes EE.
cards.head: The great swap
cards.label: THE TRAP · G and J

cards.body: The letter is named [ahsh], but inside words it makes no sound at all. Hôtel opens on the O. Heure, the hour, is [ur]. Never puff air for a French H.
cards.head: Always silent, every time
cards.label: THE TRAP · H

cards.body: Its name is [air], but the sound lives at the back of the throat, near where you gargle: a soft scrape, not the American tongue-curl. Try a gentle kh, as if lightly clearing your throat, then soften it. Feeling strange at first is completely normal.
cards.head: The throaty one
cards.label: THE TRAP · R

cards.body: English does not have it. The trick that works: say ee as in see, freeze your tongue exactly where it is, then push your lips into a tight kiss shape. Tongue says ee, lips say oo. That collision is U. It is never oo: tu is [tew], not too.
cards.head: The tight whistle vowel
cards.label: THE TRAP · U

cards.body: Worth stating because of the E and I swap: the letter I is named [ee] and usually sounds ee in words. Clean and flat, no glide.
cards.head: Just ee
cards.label: EASY WIN · I

cards.body: French borrowed W, so they literally call it double V: [DOO-bluh-vay]. Not double-you. In older borrowings it sounds like v, in newer English ones like w: le week-end.
cards.head: Double vé
cards.label: THE BORROWED ONE · W

cards.body: The name means Greek I, because the letter arrived from Greek. Say [ee-GREK]. In words it acts like a French I or a y glide.
cards.head: I grec
cards.label: THE GREEK ONE · Y

cards.body: The name is [zed], like British English, never American zee.
cards.head: Zède
cards.label: THE LAST ONE · Z

sections.title: The letters that ambush you

sections.say: English vowel letters are lazy and change constantly. French vowels are stable and clean. Tap any row to open that vowel's card and hear it. Your English autopilot will read A as ay, I as eye and E as ee. All three are wrong in French. Retrain them: A is ah, E is uh, I is ee.

detail.body: French A is an open, pure ah, as in father. Never the English ay. Ami, the friend, is [ah-MEE].
detail.title: A is [ah]

detail.body: A soft uh with a relaxed mouth, often nearly silent inside words. The English ee belongs to the letter I. Le is [luh].
detail.title: E is [uh]

detail.body: A clean, flat ee with no glide. English I is a diphthong, eye. French I never glides. Ici, here, is [ee-SEE].
detail.title: I is [ee]

detail.body: Similar to English, but tighter, with no glide at the end. Hôtel is [oh-TELL].
detail.title: O is [oh]

detail.body: No English twin. Say ee, freeze your tongue, round your lips as if to whistle. Tu is [tew], never too.
detail.title: U is [ew]

detail.body: Named Greek I after its origin. Nothing to do with why. In words it sounds ee or glides like y: yoga, [yo-GAH].
detail.title: Y is i grec

sections.title: Vowels: French versus English

sections.say: The vocabulary bank. Five themes: greetings, food and drink, travel and town, people and home, and handy small words. Tap a theme card to open its own mini deck, then swipe through and say each word aloud. One gem to notice: aujourd'hui, today, looks terrifying but is just your friends stacked together. The O sound, the buzzy J, the throaty R, a silent H, and the U. Every scary piece is a letter you already met.
sections.title: Vocabulary bank

sections.say: This is the part that pays for the whole lesson. When French speakers spell something important on the phone, they do three things you should copy. One: they use the letter names, slowly. Two: they confirm blurry letters with a helper word, B comme Bernard, B as in Bernard. Three: for an email they name the symbols too. Let us build each piece.
steps: Use the letter NAMES, slowly. Paul becomes: [pay], [ah], [ew], [ell]. Names, not sounds.
Confirm blurry letters with a helper word, because B, C, D, G, P, T, V all rhyme on the phone. The formula is B comme Bernard: B as in Bernard. Any well-known first name works.
For an email, name the symbols too: arobase for @, point for the dot. The full list is two cards away.

sections.say: Good news: you already know the tune of the French alphabet song. It is Twinkle Twinkle Little Star, same as the English ABC song. Only the words change. Slow down at the unfamiliar ending: double vé, iks, i grec, zède. Singing it a few times is a genuinely good way to lock the order in.
sections.body:
Yes, there is a French alphabet song, and it uses the same tune as the English ABC song, which is the same tune as Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star. French children learn it exactly the way you did.

The difference is the names: a, bé, cé, dé, e, effe, gé, and so on. The ending feels different because W is double vé, Y is i grec and Z is zède, so the final stretch runs: double vé, iks, i grec, zède. It does not rhyme the way the English ending does.

Hum it a few times. The tune is muscle memory you already own; you are just swapping the words.
sections.title: The alphabet song

sections.say: Eight mistakes almost every English speaker makes, one per card. For each one you get the fix and the reason your mouth wants to make it. The reason matters: once you know why a mistake happens, you can catch yourself before it does.

cards.body: Why it happens: in English the letter E literally says ee, so your mouth defaults to it. Retrain: E is uh, I is ee.
cards.head: Calling E ee
cards.label: MISTAKE 1

cards.body: Why it happens: English I is a diphthong, eye. French vowels do not glide; I is a clean ee.
cards.head: Calling I eye
cards.label: MISTAKE 2

cards.body: Why it happens: English swaps them, G is jee and J is jay. French flips it back and softens both to the measure sound. Say: G goes AY, J goes EE.

segments.text: Bonjour !
Welcome to your very first Sons lesson. Today we take apart the French alphabet: all twenty six letters, their real names, and the sounds they make inside words.

Picture this: you are on the phone with a hotel in Lyon, spelling your email. You say the letters the English way, and the receptionist writes down something completely different. By the end of this lesson, that can never happen to you again.
One idea fixes half your mistakes: a letter has a NAME, for spelling out loud, and a SOUND, the noise it makes inside a word. They are different tools for different jobs.
Our focus today: the letter names, the traps, and spelling your own name and email aloud.
The biggest trap first. In French, the letter E is a soft uh, never ee. The letter that says ee is I. Listen: the word for I, the pronoun, is:
je
That soft ending is the French E. Now the great swap: G is zhay, J is zhee, both buzzing like the s in measure. Listen to the hard and soft G, cake then giraffe:
le gâteau, la girafe
And the silent ghost: H has a name, ahsh, but inside a word it makes no sound at all. The hotel:
l'hôtel
No puff of air. The word opens straight on the O.
Your turn. Repeat after me, slowly. First, the pronoun I:
je
Now thank you, with the French R colouring the first syllable:
merci
And the scariest-looking word that is secretly all your friends: today.
aujourd'hui
Now the payoff. Spell your own first name out loud, letter by letter, using the French names. Slowly. Remember: E is uh, I is ee.
Beautiful. Now say the French word for the at sign, the one you need for every email address:
Quick check. Which letter says ee when you spell out loud: E, or I?
And the French name for W?

Your cheat sheet: names for spelling, sounds for reading. E is uh, I is ee. G goes AY, J goes EE. H is silent. U is a rounded ee. W is double vé, Y is i grec, and the at sign is arobase. Spell your name and email out loud once before you travel, and you are ready.
Bravo, à bientôt !

lessons.intro: In French, a whole word can turn on a single vowel that English does not even have. This is the deep dive into the core French vowel sounds: why French vowels stay pure instead of sliding like English ones, and how to finally make the hardest two, the U and the two EU sounds.
lessons.title: Les voyelles, en profondeur

overview.introFr: En français, un mot entier peut basculer sur une seule voyelle que l'anglais ne possède même pas. Plongez dans les voyelles orales : pourquoi elles restent pures, et comment enfin réussir les deux plus difficiles.
overview.titleEn: French Vowels in Depth: Pure Sounds, No Gliding

sections.hint: Six anchors before we dive into the detail

cards.body: French vowels are pure and unmoving. Each one keeps a single mouth position from start to finish, with no glide, unlike English, where many vowels drift toward a second sound.
cards.head: Pure, held vowels

cards.body: Front versus back: where the tongue sits in the mouth. Spread versus rounded: whether the lips stretch wide or close into a small circle. These two axes map out the entire French vowel system.
cards.head: Two axes that organize everything

cards.body: A [a] and I [i] already exist, almost identically, in English. A great place to start, as long as you keep them pure and don't let them glide.
cards.head: A and I: the two easy vowels

cards.body: O changes sound depending on what follows it. Closed at the end of a word or before a silent letter (mot, beau), open before a pronounced consonant (porte, bonne).
cards.head: O: closed or open

cards.body: An unaccented E is a quiet schwa (le), an é is closed (été), an è or ê is open (mère). Three sounds, three possible meanings.
cards.head: E: three sounds in one letter

cards.body: U [y] and EU [ø] / [œ] have no equivalent in English. Once you've mastered them, they're what really makes a French accent land.
cards.head: U and EU: the two 100% French sounds

sections.title: The Basic Idea
The Eleven Oral Vowel Sounds, One by One

sounds.memo: Closed at the end of a word, or before a silent letter. ô, au, and eau are always closed, no exceptions at this level.
Open when a consonant is actually pronounced right after it, in the same syllable.
No English equivalent. Say 'ee', keep your tongue still, then round your lips forward as if about to whistle.
sounds.sound: no English equivalent, rounded lips with a forward tongue

sounds.memo: Say the closed é of 'été', then round your lips without moving your tongue.
Say the open è of 'mère', then round your lips without moving your tongue.

check.q: Which of these sounds already exists, almost identically, in English?
Which rule best predicts a closed O?
opts: The word ends in a pronounced consonant
The syllable is open, or ends in a silent letter

opts: A closed é, mouth almost smiling

check.q: How do you position your mouth to say U [y]?
opts: Lips relaxed, like for an A

check.q: What really distinguishes EU from OU?
opts: EU rounds the lips with the tongue forward, OU rounds the lips with the tongue back
EU and OU are exactly the same sound
OU only exists in writing, never spoken aloud
EU is always a nasal sound

cards.tip: Feel where your tongue goes: keep it all the way forward, as if saying 'ee', then round only your lips. If your tongue pulls back, you get 'tout', not 'tu'.
Put a finger on your chin: for U, the jaw barely moves. Keep your tongue pressed behind your lower teeth, not back in your throat.
The sound stays short and tense at the front of the mouth, never relaxed toward the back like 'sous'.
Aim for 'i' with rounded lips. If you feel your whole mouth pull back, you've slipped into 'vous' by mistake.

sections.title: Trap Number One: U versus OU

sections.say: Time to say the two sounds English simply doesn't have.
sections.frSub: Les deux sons les plus durs
sections.title: The Two Hardest Sounds

sounds.sub: The sound with no English equivalent, and trap number one
sounds.label: U [y]
steps: Say 'ee' [i], feel your tongue high and forward, lips spread.
Hold the 'ee', don't let your tongue move.
Slowly round your lips into an 'oo' shape, as if about to whistle.
The sound that comes out is [y], French U. Repeat: tu, la rue, la lune, le mur.

sounds.sub: The second 100% French sound, in two versions
sounds.label: EU fermé et EU ouvert
steps: Say the English word 'her', but drop the R entirely, you're left with a neutral central vowel.
Without moving your tongue, purse your lips forward into a small circle, like you're about to blow out a candle.
For the closed version [ø] (word-final): keep the circle tight, sound short and bright.
For the open version [œ] (before a consonant): relax the circle slightly, let your jaw drop a touch more.

errors.why: English vowels default to diphthongs, so the mouth glides automatically if you're not paying attention.
errors.right: Hold each French vowel flat and still, one mouth position from start to finish
errors.wrong: Gliding pure vowels like English does (é becomes 'ay-ee', o becomes 'oh-oo')

errors.why: English has no rounded front vowel, so the brain substitutes the closest sound it already knows: [u].
errors.right: [y] = tongue forward like for 'ee', lips rounded like for 'oo', both at the same time
errors.wrong: Pronouncing U [y] like the English 'oo' (tu becomes 'too')

errors.why: This is the most common vowel mistake among English speakers, because both sounds sound like a generic 'oo' to an untrained ear.
errors.right: Feel your tongue's position: forward for U, back for OU
errors.wrong: Confusing U [y] and OU [u] in real words (vu and vous, su and sous)

errors.why: English O varies with accent and rhythm, but it never carries meaning the way [o] and [ɔ] do in French.
errors.right: Closed at the end of a word or before a silent letter, open before a pronounced consonant
errors.wrong: Treating closed O and open O as one single sound (beau and bonne)

errors.why: Both sounds get reflexively pulled toward the English 'ay', which doesn't really match either one.
errors.right: é = a light smile, flat, no glide; è = the jaw drops, more open
errors.wrong: Treating closed é and open è as one single sound

errors.why: Tongue position is already close to the English 'er', only the lips still need to round.
errors.right: Add lip rounding, that's exactly what's missing
errors.wrong: Replacing EU [ø] / [œ] with the English 'er' in 'her', without rounding the lips

errors.why: French doesn't have a strong word-stress system like English, each syllable stays nearly equal.
errors.right: Keep the schwa weak, short, almost silent
errors.wrong: Stressing or lengthening the schwa the way English stresses syllables (petit becomes 'peh-TEE')

errors.why: An English-speaking reader reflexively breaks apart each letter, but these French letter groups are indivisible units.
errors.right: Both are a single fixed spelling for [o], to memorize as one unit
errors.wrong: Reading eau or au letter by letter, as three separate sounds

Apply it: a vowel plus N or M at the end of a syllable nasalizes, and the N or M stays silent.
Apply it: a doubled N or M, or an N or M followed by a vowel, blocks nasalization, both sounds are heard.
Tell masculine from feminine by nasal versus oral quality alone, as in bon and bonne.
Predict whether liaison keeps a nasal, as in un homme, or denasalizes it, as in bon ami.

cards.body: A nasal vowel is one pure sound, not a vowel plus a consonant. The rule: a vowel followed by N or M at the end of a syllable nasalizes, and that N or M stays silent. bon becomes bɔ̃, temps becomes tɑ̃.
cards.head: The basic idea and the golden rule

cards.body: Nasalization is blocked in two cases: a doubled N or M, or an N or M followed by a vowel. bonne stays bɔn, ami stays ami. In both, the consonant is fully pronounced.
cards.head: The anti-rule

cards.body: The open nasal. Spelled an, am, en, or em.
cards.head: [ɑ̃] as in temps

cards.body: The rounded nasal. Spelled on or om.
cards.head: [ɔ̃] as in bon

cards.body: The front nasal. Spelled in, im, ain, aim, ein, eim, yn, or ym.
cards.head: [ɛ̃] as in pain

cards.body: The rarest nasal. Spelled un or um. Often merges with pain's sound in casual speech.
cards.head: [œ̃] as in un

sounds.sub: Lower your soft palate while keeping your mouth in the vowel position, no consonant at all
sounds.label: How to nasalize: the soft palate technique
steps: Say 'ah' [a] normally, and notice your soft palate is raised, sealing off your nose.
Now hum 'mmm' and notice the opposite: your palate is fully lowered, all air through the nose, mouth closed.
Say 'ah' again, and this time, lower your soft palate exactly as you did for 'mmm', but keep your mouth open in the 'ah' position instead of closing it.
Air should now be escaping through both your nose and your open mouth at once. That is a nasal vowel.

sounds.sub: Check what follows: a vowel or a doubled N or M blocks the nasal
sounds.label: The anti-rule in motion
steps: As you approach a nasal word, glance ahead at the very next sound.
Consonant or silence follows: keep the nasal, say the word as spelled and nasalized.
A vowel follows, and the word is an article or number (un, mon, ton, son, bien, combien...): keep the nasal AND link the consonant forward.
A vowel follows, and the word is a fronted adjective like bon: switch to the oral, N-pronounced form, exactly as the feminine would sound.

errors.why: English always sounds its written consonants, but French nasal spelling is a signal, not a sound to produce.
errors.right: The vowel alone carries the nasality, the consonant is silent.
errors.wrong: Pronouncing the N or M inside a nasal vowel, so temps comes out sounding like tahnps.

errors.why: Learners over-apply the golden rule once they've learned it, forgetting the exceptions exist for a reason.
errors.right: N or M plus a vowel, or a doubled N or M, means oral: pronounce the consonant fully.
errors.wrong: Nasalizing words where the anti-rule blocks it, so ami sounds like ahn-mee, or bonne sounds like bohn.

errors.why: Both get flattened into one vague awn sound by an untrained English ear.
errors.right: [ɑ̃] is neutral-lipped, [ɔ̃] is rounded: genuinely different vowels, different words.
errors.wrong: Confusing [ɑ̃] and [ɔ̃], so that sans and son sound the same.

errors.why: English readers default to sounding out each letter individually.
errors.right: Both are single, fixed spellings for one nasal sound, [ɛ̃].
errors.wrong: Reading ain or ein as two separate vowel sounds.

errors.why: This exception applies to some of the most frequent words in the language, bien, rien, combien.
errors.right: en after i or y is pulled to [ɛ̃]: bien is [bjɛ̃], not [bjɑ̃].
errors.wrong: Assuming en is always [ɑ̃], even after i or y, so bien comes out sounding like byahn.

errors.why: This is genuine grammar hiding inside pronunciation, not a random performance detail.
errors.right: Articles and numbers usually keep the nasal and link, as in un homme, while a small set of pre-posed adjectives denasalize, as in bon ami.
errors.wrong: Treating every nasal-plus-vowel-initial-word boundary the same way.

errors.why: Treating a live sound change as either wrong or the only correct form both cause confusion. It's genuinely a spectrum across speakers and regions.
errors.right: Learn the distinct [œ̃] first, and recognize that many speakers merge it into [ɛ̃] in casual speech. Both are fine to understand and produce.
errors.wrong: Assuming [œ̃] must always sound identical to [ɛ̃], or always keeping them artificially separate even in casual contexts.

errors.why: Written French marks gender with extra letters, spoken French frequently marks it with nasality alone.
errors.right: Give the nasal or oral contrast the same care you'd give any other grammar rule, it changes meaning, not just accent.
errors.wrong: Forgetting that nasal versus oral is often the only spoken signal of grammatical gender, as in américain versus américaine.

sections.body: You just mastered the one feature of French that English has no equivalent for at all: four pure vowel sounds carried entirely through the nose. That skill alone unlocks an entire hidden layer of French grammar you could not hear before.
sections.title: The nasals are yours
points: You can produce all four nasal vowel qualities: [ɑ̃] in temps, [ɔ̃] in bon, [ɛ̃] in pain, and [œ̃] in un.
You apply the golden rule automatically: a vowel plus N or M at the end of a syllable nasalizes, and the N or M disappears.
You catch the anti-rule every time: a doubled N or M, or an N or M followed by a vowel, keeps both sounds oral.
You hear grammatical gender that used to be invisible, in pairs like bon and bonne, un and une, américain and américaine.
You predict liaison correctly, keeping the nasal in un homme and denasalizing bon ami.
This closes out the Sons unit. Your next stop is A1.

lessons.intro: You order « un café » with confidence, but the barista pauses for half a second. Most French consonants are exactly like English. This lesson isolates the handful that are not: the throaty R, the soft J, the two-sound C and G, and the CH, GN, QU, PH, TH spellings, so you can read any word and already know which sound to make.
lessons.title: Les consonnes françaises

overview.subFr: Les consonnes : ce qui change vraiment
overview.introFr: La plupart des consonnes françaises ressemblent à l’anglais. Ce cours isole celles qui diffèrent vraiment : le R du fond de la gorge, le J adouci, la règle à deux sons du C et du G, et les groupes CH, GN, QU, PH, TH.
overview.titleEn: French Consonants: The Sounds That Actually Differ

sections.say: Picture this. You order a coffee with total confidence, but the barista pauses for half a second before understanding you. Here is the reassuring part: most French consonants are nearly identical to English. B, D, F, L, M, N, P, T, V, Z, say them the way you already do. This lesson is a short, closed list of exceptions, not a whole new system.
sections.body:
You say « un café, s’il vous plaît » with confidence, but the barista hesitates before understanding you. Your C slipped toward an S, and your R never left the tip of your tongue.

The good news: most French consonants are nearly identical to English. B, D, F, L, M, N, P, T, V, Z sound the way you already say them. This lesson is not a new consonant system, it is a short, closed list of exceptions to the one you already have.
sections.title: Why this matters

sections.say: By the end of this lesson you can produce the throat R and soft J, apply the C and G rule from spelling alone, read every forced-spelling override, and handle CH, GN, QU, PH, TH and silent H on sight.
sections.title: What you’ll master
points: Produce the throat R instead of an English or Spanish-style R.
Produce soft French J, and hear why soft G makes the identical sound.
Apply the C rule (hard before a, o, u, soft before e, i, y) on sight.
Apply the matching G rule, plus the three forced-spelling overrides: ç, gu, ge.
Read CH, GN, QU, PH, TH and silent H correctly, every time.
Tell which ten consonants need zero new muscle memory.

sections.say: Three buckets. Bucket one is unchanged from English, nothing to learn. Bucket two is a new but fixed sound: R, J, CH, GN, QU, PH, TH, H. Bucket three is a letter that switches sound depending on what follows it: C and G. Today lives almost entirely in buckets two and three.
sections.body:
Every French consonant sorts into one of three buckets. Bucket one: unchanged from English, no new skill, that’s B D F L M N P T V Z. Bucket two: a genuinely different but fixed sound, no ambiguity once learned, that’s R, J, CH, GN, QU, PH, TH, H. Bucket three: a letter that switches between two sounds depending on the next letter, that’s C and G.

This lesson spends almost all its time in buckets two and three, because that’s where every real mistake lives.
sections.title: The three buckets

sections.say: Five letters, one grid. Tap any letter to open its card: its French name, the sound it makes inside words, and an example. C and G each carry two sounds, that’s worth extra attention, and it’s exactly what the next few cards go deep on.
sections.title: R, J, H, C, G: the five letters that ambush you

letters.memo: Not the American tongue-curl, not the Spanish trill. Build it from a relaxed hard G.
letters.name: [air]
letters.sound: a soft, throaty scrape from the very back of the mouth

letters.memo: A pure hiss, voiced. No hidden d at the front.
letters.name: [zhee]
letters.sound: the buzzy zh of measure, never the English hard j

letters.memo: A name, but never a sound. No puff of air, ever.
letters.name: [ahsh]

letters.memo: Ç forces the soft s even in front of a, o, u: garçon.
letters.name: [say]
letters.sound: k before a, o, u; s before e, i, y

letters.name: [zhay]
letters.sound: hard g before a, o, u; soft zh before e, i, y

sections.say: The single most useful rule in this lesson. C and G both flip sound depending on the very next letter. A, o, u keeps them hard. E, i, y makes them soft. Tap any row for the detail, and watch the third and sixth rows: ç and gu are how French forces the “wrong” sound on purpose.

detail.body: A hard k. Café, comme, cuir.
detail.title: C before a, o, u

detail.body: A soft s. Ce, ici, cycle.
detail.title: C before e, i, y

detail.body: The cedilla forces a soft s even in front of a, o, u: garçon, français.
detail.title: Ç overrides the rule

detail.body: A hard g. Gare, gomme, aigu.
detail.title: G before a, o, u

detail.body: A soft zh, identical to J. Gel, gilet, gym.
detail.title: G before e, i, y

detail.body: A silent u forces a hard g even before e or i: guerre, guitare.
detail.title: GU overrides the rule

sections.title: C and G: the two-sound gate

sections.say: Three override spellings do all the work: ç forces a soft sound before a, o, u. Gu forces a hard sound before e, i. Ge forces a soft sound before a, o. Once you see them as a permission slip rather than an exception, they stop needing memorization word by word.

cards.body: Both hard g. The silent u in guerre exists for one reason: to keep the g hard in front of e.
cards.head: gare vs guerre

cards.body: Gel is the regular soft g before e. Guitare is the forced hard g, thanks to that same silent u.
cards.head: gel vs guitare

cards.body: Café is the regular hard c before a. Garçon needs the cedilla to force the c soft in front of o.
cards.head: café vs garçon

cards.body: GE keeps a G soft in front of a or o, by inserting a silent e. Same idea as gu, opposite direction.
cards.head: The mirror trick

sections.say: CH and GN behave as single, indivisible units. CH is always the plain sh sound. GN is always one merged nasal sound, never a hard g followed by a separate n.

sections.say: A simple scanning habit turns this rule from a guess into a reflex. Spot every C and G, check the next letter, watch for the three override spellings, then speak. A few days of doing this on short phrases and it becomes automatic.

Check the very next letter. A, O, U or a consonant means hard. E, I, Y means soft.

sections.say: Four borrowed spellings, each simplified to one clean sound. QU is k, never a kw glide. PH is f. TH is t. And H, no matter where it sits, makes no sound at all.

detail.body: French has no equivalent of the English th in think. Thé, théâtre.
detail.title: TH is always t

cards.body: Café is hard, ce is soft. The rule is fully predictable, there’s never a real reason to guess.

cards.body: Gare is hard, gel is soft. G follows the identical rule as C, one letter later in the alphabet.

sections.say: Bravo. Before the quiz, your key takeaways. Ten letters need nothing new. R is a throat scrape. J and soft G are the same buzzy sound. C and G both flip on the next letter, and ç, gu, ge are the built-in overrides. Ready? The quiz is one tap away.
sections.body: Bravo. You just isolated the handful of French consonants that genuinely differ from English, and left the other ten alone. R lives in the throat, J and soft G buzz like measure, and C and G both flip on the very next letter. One short quiz stands between you and the finish line.
sections.title: Round-up
points: Ten letters transfer free: B, D, F, L, M, N, P, T, V, Z.
R is a throat scrape, never the tongue tip.
J and soft G are the exact same buzzy sound, two spellings.
C and G both flip on the next letter: a, o, u is hard, e, i, y is soft.
Ç forces soft, GU forces hard, GE forces soft. The rule’s built-in overrides.
CH is sh, GN is one merged sound, QU is k, PH is f, TH is t, H is silent.

questions.q: How does French force a hard [g] before e or i, as in guerre?
questions.why: The silent u in gu is a permission slip, not a sound.
opts: By adding a silent u: gu

questions.q: What does CH normally sound like?
questions.why: French almost never uses the hard English ch sound.

questions.q: How is GN pronounced, as in montagne?
questions.why: GN functions as a single consonant, not two letters in sequence.

questions.q: How is quatre pronounced?
questions.why: French QU is just k. English “kw” never appears.

questions.q: Is H ever pronounced in French?
questions.why: H is always silent, whether it opens a word or sits mid-word.

questions.why: The cedilla overrides the normal hard-before-o rule.

questions.q: Which sentence uses both the C/G rule and a forced-spelling override?
questions.why: Ce is soft C by the regular rule; guerre is a forced hard G via gu.

segments.text: Bonjour !
Welcome back to Sons. Today, French consonants, the ones that actually differ from English.

You already know ten of them by heart: B, D, F, L, M, N, P, T, V, Z. This lesson isolates the handful that don’t transfer: the throaty R, the soft J, the two-sound C and G, and four borrowed spellings.
One useful reframe before we start. You are not learning a new consonant system. You are learning a short, closed list of exceptions to the one you already have.
Today’s focus: R, J, the C and G rule, and CH, GN, QU, PH, TH, H.
Start with R. Say an English hard g, back of the mouth. Now let a little air rasp through instead of closing fully. That controlled scrape is the French R.
la rue
The street. All throat, no tongue tip. Now the soft J: isolate the buzzy middle sound of the English word measure.
je
I. No hard d at the front, just the buzz. And that same buzz is exactly what soft G sounds like too.
le gel
The gel. Now the rule that runs all of this: C and G each carry two sounds, and the very next letter decides which. A, o, u keeps them hard. E, i, y makes them soft.
le café, ce
Coffee, this. Hard, then soft. Same letter, two jobs.
Your turn. Repeat after me, slowly. The street:
la rue
Now the boy, where the cedilla forces the c soft even before o:
le garçon
And the cat, a plain sh, never the English ch:
le chat
Now say this sentence on your own, slowly. Watch the G twice, hard, then soft.
Un grand garçon regarde la guitare.

segments.expected: Un grand garçon regarde la guitare.

segments.text: Now the mountain, one merged sound for GN, not two:
Quick check. Before a, o or u, is C hard or soft?
And what does the cedilla, ç, force?

Your cheat sheet. Ten letters transfer free: B, D, F, L, M, N, P, T, V, Z. R lives in the throat. J and soft G buzz like measure. C and G both flip on the very next letter: a, o, u keeps them hard, e, i, y makes them soft, and ç, gu, ge are the overrides. CH is sh. GN is one sound. QU is k. PH is f. TH is t. H is always silent.
Bravo, à bientôt !

lessons.intro: French has four ways to say « the », and the choice depends on the noun’s gender, number, and first letter. There is no way around them — every noun you ever use will need one.

items.fr: Elle se réveille tôt et elle se lève sans bruit.
items.en: She wakes up early and gets up quietly.
items.ipa: ɛl sə ʁe.vɛj to e ɛl sə lɛv sɑ̃ bʁɥi
items.notes: “tôt” has a circumflex; it is not the same word as “taux”.

items.fr: Les élèves écoutent attentivement la maîtresse.
items.en: The students listen attentively to the teacher.
items.notes: “maîtresse” keeps the circumflex from “maître”, even with the feminine ending.

items.fr: Le panda se nourrit presque uniquement de bambou.
items.en: The panda feeds almost exclusively on bamboo.

items.fr: Il faut qu'elle organise mieux ses journées si elle veut tout finir.
items.en: She needs to organize her days better if she wants to finish everything.
items.ipa: il fo kɛl ɔʁ.ɡa.niz mjø se ʒuʁ.ne si ɛl vø tu fi.niʁ
items.notes: “Il faut que” requires the subjunctive “organise”.

items.fr: Je prends un café noir le matin.
items.en: I have a black coffee in the morning.
items.ipa: ʒə pʁɑ̃ œ̃ ka.fe nwaʁ lə ma.tɛ̃
items.notes: The final letters of “prends” are silent, even though they're written.

items.fr: Elle a commandé un café allongé sans sucre.
items.en: She ordered a long black coffee without sugar.
items.ipa: ɛl a kɔ.mɑ̃.de œ̃ ka.fe a.lɔ̃.ʒe sɑ̃ sykʁ
items.notes: “Commandé” ends in é because it follows “a” in the passé composé.

items.fr: Nous buvons notre café sur la terrasse quand il fait beau.
items.en: We drink our coffee on the terrace when the weather's nice.
items.ipa: nu by.vɔ̃ nɔtʁ ka.fe syʁ la tɛ.ʁas kɑ̃.t‿il fɛ bo
items.notes: “Quand il” is linked by a liaison, pronounced “kɑ̃.t‿il”.

items.fr: Ce café reste bondé bien qu'il y ait moins de touristes cet été.
items.en: This café stays packed even though there are fewer tourists this summer.
items.ipa: sə ka.fe ʁɛst bɔ̃.de bjɛ̃ kil j‿ɛ mwɛ̃ də tu.ʁist sɛ.t‿e.te
items.notes: “Ait”, the subjunctive of avoir, sounds like “est” but is spelled differently after “bien que”.

items.fr: C'est le seul café du quartier où l'on peut encore fumer en terrasse.
items.en: It's the only café in the neighborhood where you can still smoke on the terrace.
items.ipa: sɛ lə sœl ka.fe dy kaʁ.tje u lɔ̃ pø ɑ̃.kɔʁ fy.me ɑ̃ tɛ.ʁas
items.notes: “Où l'on” uses the elided “l'” before “on” for a smoother sound.

items.fr: La maison est grande et blanche.
items.en: The house is big and white.
items.ipa: la mɛ.zɔ̃ ɛ ɡʁɑ̃d e blɑ̃ʃ
items.notes: “Grande” and “blanche” take the feminine ending to agree with “maison”.

items.fr: Nous avons repeint les volets en vert cet été.
items.en: We repainted the shutters green this summer.
items.ipa: nu.z‿a.vɔ̃ ʁə.pɛ̃ le vɔ.lɛ ɑ̃ vɛʁ sɛ.t‿e.te
items.notes: “Repeint” stays invariable even though “volets” is plural, since the object follows the verb.

items.fr: Le grenier est plein de vieux cartons poussiéreux.
items.en: The attic is full of old, dusty boxes.
items.ipa: lə ɡʁə.nje ɛ plɛ̃ də vjø kaʁ.tɔ̃ pu.sje.ʁø
items.notes: The final “x” of “vieux” is silent.

items.fr: Ils ont fait construire une véranda derrière la maison.
items.en: They had a veranda built behind the house.
items.ipa: il.z‿ɔ̃ fɛ kɔ̃s.tʁɥiʁ yn ve.ʁɑ̃.da dɛ.ʁjɛʁ la mɛ.zɔ̃
items.notes: “Fait” stays invariable in this causative construction with “construire”.

items.fr: La maison qu'ils ont achetée a besoin de gros travaux.
items.en: The house they bought needs major renovations.
items.ipa: la mɛ.zɔ̃ ki.l‿ɔ̃.t‿a.ʃə.te a bə.zwɛ̃ də ɡʁo tʁa.vo
items.notes: “Achetée” agrees in the feminine with “maison”, the preceding direct object.

items.fr: Je me lève à sept heures tous les jours.
items.en: I get up at seven every day.
items.ipa: ʒə mə lɛv a sɛ.t‿œʁ tu le ʒuʁ
items.notes: “Lève” takes an accent grave because the stem vowel is stressed, unlike in “lever”.

items.fr: D'habitude, je me douche avant de prendre mon petit-déjeuner.
items.en: I usually shower before having breakfast.
items.ipa: da.by.tyd ʒə mə duʃ a.vɑ̃ də pʁɑ̃dʁ mɔ̃ pə.ti de.ʒœ.ne
items.notes: “D'habitude” elides “de” before the vowel of “habitude”.

items.fr: Le soir, ils regardent les informations avant de se coucher.
items.en: In the evening, they watch the news before going to bed.
items.ipa: lə swaʁ il ʁə.ɡaʁd le.z‿ɛ̃.fɔʁ.ma.sjɔ̃ a.vɑ̃ də sə ku.ʃe
items.notes: “Informations” is almost always used in the plural in French, unlike its English equivalent.

items.fr: Depuis qu'elle travaille de nuit, ses horaires ont complètement changé.
items.en: Since she started working nights, her schedule has changed completely.
items.ipa: də.pɥi kɛl tʁa.vaj də nɥi se.z‿ɔ.ʁɛʁ ɔ̃ kɔ̃.plɛt.mɑ̃ ʃɑ̃.ʒe
items.notes: “Ses horaires” is plural, so it takes “ses” rather than the singular “son”.

items.fr: Elle fait de la natation trois fois par semaine.
items.en: She goes swimming three times a week.
items.ipa: ɛl fɛ də la na.ta.sjɔ̃ tʁwa fwa paʁ sə.mɛn
items.notes: “Fois” is invariable and never takes an s, even after “trois”.

items.fr: Nous avons couru un marathon l'année dernière.
items.en: We ran a marathon last year.
items.ipa: nu.z‿a.vɔ̃ ku.ʁy œ̃ ma.ʁa.tɔ̃ la.ne dɛʁ.njɛʁ
items.notes: “Couru” is the irregular past participle of “courir”, not “couri”.

items.fr: Bien qu'elle se soit entraînée tous les jours, elle n'a pas gagné la course.
items.en: Even though she trained every day, she didn't win the race.
items.ipa: bjɛ̃.kɛl sə swa.t‿ɑ̃.tʁɛ.ne tu le ʒuʁ ɛl na pa ɡa.ɲe la kuʁs
items.notes: “Entraînée” agrees with the feminine subject because the reflexive pronoun acts as the object.

items.fr: Les randonneurs se sont perdus dans le brouillard pendant deux heures.
items.en: The hikers got lost in the fog for two hours.
items.ipa: le ʁɑ̃.dɔ.nœʁ sə sɔ̃ pɛʁ.dy dɑ̃ lə bʁu.jaʁ pɑ̃.dɑ̃ dø.z‿œʁ
items.notes: “Perdus” takes the masculine plural ending to agree with “les randonneurs”.

items.fr: Mon sac est resté dans le bus.
items.en: My bag stayed on the bus.
items.ipa: mɔ̃ sak ɛ ʁɛs.te dɑ̃ lə bys
items.notes: “Est” sounds like “ait”, but only “est” fits after “sac”.

items.fr: Ce stylo n'écrit plus très bien.
items.en: This pen doesn't write very well anymore.
items.ipa: sə sti.lo ne.kʁi ply tʁɛ bjɛ̃
items.notes: “N'écrit” elides “ne” before the vowel of “écrit”.

items.fr: Elle a rangé ses clés dans le tiroir du bureau.
items.en: She put her keys away in the desk drawer.
items.ipa: ɛl.z‿a ʁɑ̃.ʒe se kle dɑ̃ lə ti.ʁwaʁ dy by.ʁo
items.notes: “Ses clés” is plural, so it takes “ses” rather than the singular “sa”.

items.fr: Le vase en verre s'est cassé en tombant.
items.en: The glass vase broke when it fell.
items.ipa: lə vaz ɑ̃ vɛʁ sɛ ka.se ɑ̃ tɔ̃.bɑ̃
items.notes: “S'est cassé” uses être because it's a reflexive verb, not avoir.

items.fr: Le marchand vend des fraises fraîches ce matin.
items.en: The vendor is selling fresh strawberries this morning.
items.ipa: lə maʁ.ʃɑ̃ vɑ̃ de fʁɛz fʁɛʃ sə ma.tɛ̃
items.notes: “Ce” and “se” sound alike, but only “ce matin” fits as a demonstrative here.

items.fr: Les prix du marché ont un peu baissé cette semaine.
items.en: Market prices have gone down a little this week.
items.ipa: le pʁi dy maʁ.ʃe ɔ̃.t‿œ̃ pø bɛ.se sɛt sə.mɛn
items.notes: “Ont un” requires a liaison, pronounced “ɔ̃.t‿œ̃”.

items.fr: Elle a acheté un panier plein de tomates bien mûres.
items.en: She bought a basket full of nice, ripe tomatoes.
items.ipa: ɛl.z‿a a.ʃə.te œ̃ pa.nje plɛ̃ də tɔ.mat bjɛ̃ myʁ
items.notes: “Mûres” agrees in the feminine plural with “tomates”.

The “t” of “comment” is pronounced as a liaison before the vowel in “allez”.

items.en: Hi, are you doing well today?
items.notes: The “h” in “aujourd'hui” is silent, and the word is never split despite the apostrophe.

items.fr: Nous nous sommes vus hier soir, c'était sympa.
items.en: We saw each other last night, it was nice.
items.ipa: nu nu sɔm vy jɛʁ swaʁ, se.tɛ sɛ̃.pa
items.notes: “vus” takes a plural “s” because the reflexive pronoun “nous” acts as the agreeing direct object.

items.fr: Excusez-moi, est-ce que vous avez l'heure ?
items.en: Excuse me, do you have the time?
items.notes: “l'heure” elides “la” before the silent “h” of “heure”.

items.fr: Ma sœur est plus jeune que moi.
items.en: My sister is younger than me.
items.ipa: ma sœʁ ɛ ply ʒœn kə mwa
items.notes: “sœur” is spelled with the œ ligature, never “oe” or “eu”.

items.fr: Mon père travaille tous les jours sauf le dimanche.
items.en: My father works every day except Sunday.
items.ipa: mɔ̃ pɛʁ tʁa.vaj tu le ʒuʁ sof lə di.mɑ̃ʃ
items.notes: The “s” in “tous” is silent here because it precedes “les jours”; it's only pronounced when “tous” stands alone.

items.fr: Mes parents sont nés en Belgique.
items.en: My parents were born in Belgium.
items.ipa: me pa.ʁɑ̃ sɔ̃ ne ɑ̃ bɛl.ʒik
items.notes: “nés” takes an “s” because the passé composé with “être” agrees with the plural subject “mes parents”.

items.fr: Ma tante habite à côté de chez nous.
items.en: My aunt lives right next door to us.
items.ipa: ma tɑ̃t a.bit a ko.te də ʃe nu
items.notes: “à” needs a grave accent here since it's the preposition, not the verb “a” from avoir.

items.fr: Mes grands-parents se sont mariés il y a cinquante ans.
items.en: My grandparents got married fifty years ago.
items.ipa: me ɡʁɑ̃.pa.ʁɑ̃ sə sɔ̃ ma.ʁje il i a sɛ̃.kɑ̃t ɑ̃
items.notes: “il y a” never takes an apostrophe, even though it's sometimes mispronounced as if it did.
